_README: Every file under public/ must appear here, matched by exact path or by a glob; an exact path wins. `npm run lint` fails on any file that does not. `ship: false` marks an asset that may not be published — the licence check run with --publish fails while any of those are still in the tree. This file exists because the project already lost a full voice-over to a licence nobody checked.

public/vo/six-wives.wav.source: Generated by tools/tts.py (`npm run tts -- six-wives`), Kokoro-82M
public/vo/six-wives.wav.note: Kokoro-82M is Apache-2.0 and runs locally, so the read carries a commercial licence. Replaced a free-plan ElevenLabs render that did not. Regenerating rewrites the word timings, so both Tudor shorts re-cut themselves against the new read — check their beats after, which is what docs/vo-licensing.md describes.

public/sfx/*.wav.note: Synthesised from numpy rather than sourced, so there is no provenance to verify: the only thing to audit is tools/sfx.py. Deterministic — re-running rewrites every sound byte for byte. Replaced free-plan ElevenLabs renders, which carried no commercial licence.

public/vo/*.wav.source: Synthesised locally with Kokoro-82M (hexgrad/Kokoro-82M) via tools/tts.py
public/vo/*.wav.note: Apache-2.0 model run on our own machine: no per-character cost and no terms page that can change under a published video. The exact entry for six-wives.wav above overrides this one until that file is replaced.

public/fonts/*.source: Copied unmodified from the Debian fonts-liberation (Liberation 2.1) and fonts-inter (Inter 4.0) packages, with each package's copyright file as LICENSE-*.txt beside them
public/fonts/*.note: The faces the cloud renderer was already substituting for Arial Black, Arial, Georgia and Helvetica Neue, pinned so that every machine draws what QA measured. OFL allows bundling with the project; only selling the fonts on their own, or a modified copy under the reserved names, is ruled out. See src/fonts.ts.

It is a real person's hand, face not shown: fine for editorial use like this. 1280px rendition. Fetched from Wikimedia Commons on 2026-11-10; licence as stated on the file's page that day. Checked again 2026-11-18: the Unsplash file name the Commons page records, photo-1491743715344, is the upload time in Unix milliseconds, 2017-04-09 13:15 UTC, before Unsplash dropped CC0 in June 2017; a CC0 dedication cannot be withdrawn.

public/3d/cleopatra-world.mp4.source: Own work: rendered with Blender 5.3 (Cycles, Metal GPU) by tools/blender/cleopatra_world.py. Shapes are procedural. Surfaces use six CC0 texture scans from Poly Haven (polyhaven.com), fetched by tools/blender/fetch_assets.sh: aerial_beach_01 and sandstone_blocks_05 (Rob Tuytel), dense_sand (Dimitrios Savva), sandy_gravel_02 (Dario Barresi), rock_face_03 (Dario Barresi, Rico Cilliers), rough_linen (colormass, Rico Cilliers). The people are MakeHuman bodies, skins and eyes (MakeHuman system assets, CC0, makehumancommunity.org), shaped, posed and dressed by tools/blender/make_people.py with the MPFB 2.0.18 add-on; their clothes are modelled in that script.
public/3d/cleopatra-world.mp4.note: Blender and MPFB are GPL; the GPL covers the programs, not the images they render, which belong to whoever made them (see blender.org/about/license). Poly Haven and MakeHuman system assets are CC0: no credit required, given anyway. No other downloaded models. Frames 150-1994 of the cleopatra-pyramid edit, 30 fps.

public/img/cleopatra-berlin.jpg.source: Marble portrait head of Cleopatra VII, 1st century BC, Antikensammlung Berlin, inv. 1976.10 (shown in the Altes Museum), the 'Berlin Cleopatra'; photograph by Louis le Grand — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kleopatra-VII.-Altes-Museum-Berlin1.jpg
public/img/cleopatra-berlin.jpg.note: The photographer released the photo into the public domain on Commons; the sculpture is ancient. The file used is the current Commons revision, a 2012 noise-reduction and contrast overwrite of the 2007 photo by Commons user Arbeiterreserve, on the same public-domain page. Dating disagrees between sources: the museum's catalogue record (recherche.smb.museum/detail/677025) gives the third quarter of the 1st century BC, 'um 50 – 38 v. Chr.' (as read by A7 pass 6); the Commons description gives ca. 40-30 BC. On screen it says only '1st century BC', which both support. Credited on screen anyway.
